Consumerism. It's both a socioeconomic phenomenon and an artistic subject that modern and contemporary artists have interrogated, celebrated, and critiqued. The twentieth-century rise of mass production, advertising, and consumer culture became a central preoccupation of pop art, which treated brand names, commercial packaging, and mass-manufactured objects as subjects worthy of fine art.

Consumerism emerged as a dominant economic and cultural force in the early twentieth century, especially after industrialization and mass marketing. It treated consumer goods and brand identity as sources of meaning, status, and self-definition within modern societies. Pop artists elevated soup cans, Coca-Cola bottles, and celebrity images to the status of art. Andy Warhol became the principal voice, treating mass-produced commercial imagery like Campbell's Soup and Marilyn Monroe as worthy of fine art reproduction via silkscreen.

This challenged the Romantic and Modernist hierarchies that separated high art from low commercial culture. The nineteen twenties witnessed consumerism's cultural peak, when advertising, mass production, and disposability became ideals rather than concerns. Contemporary art continues to wrestle with consumerism, asking questions of authenticity, reproducibility, and the artist's role in a market-saturated world. Consumerism marks the boundary between art and everyday commerce, raising fundamental questions about taste, authenticity, and cultural value.
